We have a task: identify the organic compound from experimental data. We have mass spec: m/z 193.11027872702 (intensity 100) etc. So molecular ion at 193.1103. Need to deduce formula. Use accurate mass to get formula. Let's compute possible formula. Use typical elements C, H, O. 193.1103. Let's approximate: C11H?O? Let's compute mass of C11H12O3: C11=132.0, H12=12.0936, O3=47.9847 total = 192.0783? Wait compute: atomic masses: C 12.0000, H 1.007825, O 15.994915. So C11 = 132.0000, H12 = 12.0939, O3 = 47.9847 => total 192.0786. Not 193.11. C12H12O3: C12=144, H12=12.094, O3=47.985 => 204.079. Too high. C10H12O4: C10=120, H12=12.094, O4=63.9797 => 196.074. Slight high. C11H14O2: 132+14.1095+31.9898=178.0993. Not. C10H14O3: 120+14.1095+47.9847=182.0942. Not. C9H10O4: 108+10.078+63.9797=182.058. Not. Need 193.1103. Let's try C11H14O3: 132+14.1095+47.9847=194.0942. Slight high. C12H12O2: 144+12.094+31.9898=188.0838. Not. C13H12O2: 156+12.094+31.9898=200.0838. Not.

Maybe includes nitrogen? But mass spec shows isotopic pattern typical for C, H, O. Let's compute exact mass for C11H12O4: 132+12.094+63.9797=208.074. Not.

C10H12O3: 120+12.094+47.985=180.079. Not.

C9H12O5: 108+12.094+79.9746=200.069. Not.

C8H8O6: 96+8.0626+95.9695=200.032. Not.

Maybe formula C11H12O3 gave 192.0786, but observed 193.1103, difference ~1.0317, which is about mass of hydrogen (1.0078) plus maybe extra 0.0239 (C13? no). Could be C11H13O3? mass = 132+13.101+47.985=193.086. That's close: 193.086 vs 193.1103 diff 0.0243. Could be C10H13O4: 120+13.101+63.9797=197.0807. Not.

C12H13O2: 144+13.101+31.9898=189.0908. Not.

C9H13O5: 108+13.101+79.9746=201.0756.

So likely formula C11H13O3 (exact mass 193.086). Observed 193.1103, 0.0243 higher. Could be due to measurement error? But high-res mass likely accurate within few ppm. Let's compute ppm error: (0.0243/193.086)*1e6 = 126 ppm, too high. Maybe formula C10H13O4? mass 120+13.101+63.9797=197.0807, not.

Maybe includes chlorine? Cl 34.9694. C9H9ClO2: 108+9.070+70.9388=188.009. Not.

Maybe includes sulfur? S 31.9721. C9H10SO3: 108+10.078+31.972+47.985=197. (not). Not.

Let's compute exact mass for C12H16O3: 144+16.125+47.985=208.11.

Our observed 193.1103 could be C9H13NO3? N 14.0031. mass =108+13.101+14.003+47.985=183.089. Not.

C10H13NO3: 120+13.101+14.003+47.985=195.089. Not.

C11H13O3 seems plausible but mass off.

Let's compute exact mass for C11H13O3 using high precision: C 12.000000, H 1.0078250321, O 15.9949146221.

C11 = 132.000000
H13 = 13.1017254173
O3 = 47.9847438663
Sum = 193.0864692836

Observed 193.11027872702 diff = 0.0238094434.

Maybe formula C10H13O4? compute: C10=120, H13=13.1017, O4=63.97966 => 197.0814 diff 3.97.

C12H13O2: 144+13.1017+31.9898=189.0915 diff -4.

C9H13O5: 108+13.1017+79.9746=201.0763 diff 7.966.

Thus maybe measurement includes sodium adduct [M+Na]+? m/z 193 could be M+Na? If M+Na = 193.110, then M = 170.1 (193.110 - 22.9898 = 170.120). That would correspond to formula C10H14O2? compute: 120+14.1095+31.9898=166.0993. Not.

Or M+H? m/z 193.110 as [M+H]+ then neutral mass = 192.1025. That matches C11H12O3 (192.0786) diff 0.0239 again.

So maybe the ion is [M+Na]+? Let's compute M neutral 170.120. Could be C9H14O3? mass =108+14.1095+47.985=170.0945 close diff 0.0255. So maybe [M+Na]+ of C9H14O3. That would give m/z 193.0843? Wait add Na 22.9898 => 193.0843, observed 193.1103 diff 0.026. So similar.

Thus ambiguous.

We have carbon NMR data: Deltas: 166.40, 144.78, 132.00, 130.07, 130.07, 127.80, 127.80, 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23.

That's 11 carbons. So formula likely C11 something. Good.

We have 11 carbon signals, matches C11. So formula C11H?O?. The carbonyl carbon at 166.4 suggests ester or acid. Aromatic carbons around 130-144. Two signals at 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23 likely aliphatic.

Thus maybe compound is methyl 4-methoxy cinnamate? That's C11H12O3? Wait methyl p-methoxycinnamate: formula C11H12O3? Actually cinnamic acid methyl ester (methyl cinnamate) is C10H10O2? Let's compute: C10H10O2 = 162.07. Not.

p-Methoxy cinnamic acid (p-methoxycinnamic acid) formula C11H10O3? Actually C11H10O3 = 194.058? Let's compute: C11=132, H10=10.078, O3=47.985 => 190.063. Not.

Our carbon NMR shows two methoxy groups? 52.24 and 49.55 maybe OCH3 (around 55 ppm). 52 is typical for OCH3. 49 maybe CH2 attached to O? 43 maybe CH2 next to carbonyl. 19 is methyl.

Thus maybe compound is ethyl 4-methoxybenzoate? That's C9H10O3? Wait ethyl p-methoxybenzoate formula C9? Actually p-anisic acid ethyl ester: C10H12O3? Let's compute: C10=120, H12=12.094, O3=47.985 => 180.079. Not.

Our carbon count 11 suggests maybe methyl 4-methoxybenzoate (anisic acid methyl ester) C9? Actually anisic acid methyl ester: C9? Let's compute: anisic acid (p-methoxybenzoic acid) C8H8O3? Wait p-methoxybenzoic acid: C8? Actually benzene ring (C6) + COOH (C1) + OCH3 (C1) = C8? plus? Let's compute: C6 (ring) + 1 carbonyl carbon + 1 methoxy carbon = C8. So formula C8H8O3? Not.

But we have 11 carbons, maybe dimethyl ester of something.

Let's examine carbon NMR: aromatic carbons: 144.78 (likely aromatic carbon attached to OMe), 132, 130.07 (two same), 127.80 (two same). That's 6 aromatic carbons (makes sense for monosubstituted phenyl). So phenyl ring with one substituent (maybe OMe). The carbonyl at 166.4 (ester). Then OCH3 at 52.24. Then maybe another OCH3 at 49.55? But OCH3 usually ~55. 49 could be CH2 attached to O (like O-CH2-). 43.55 maybe CH2 next to carbonyl (alpha). 19.23 is methyl (maybe CH3 attached to carbonyl? like acetyl). So maybe compound is methyl 4-methoxyphenylacetate? That would have aromatic ring (6 C), carbonyl carbon (1), OCH3 (1), CH2 (1), CH3 (1) = total 10? Wait count: phenyl (6), carbonyl carbon (1) =7, OCH3 (1) =8, CH2 (1) =9, CH3 (1) =10. Need 11. Maybe there is another OCH3 (dimethyl). Could be methyl 4-methoxyphenylacetate (C10H12O3). That's 10 carbons, not 11.

Our carbon count 11 suggests maybe phenyl ring (6), carbonyl (1), OCH3 (1), OCH2CH3 (2) = total 10? Actually ethoxy group adds 2 carbons (CH2, CH3). So methyl 4-methoxybenzoate (anisic acid methyl ester) has phenyl (6), carbonyl (1), OCH3 (1), OCH3 on ring (1) = 9? Wait OCH3 on ring is carbon, yes. So total 6+1+1+1=9. Not 11.

Maybe compound is dimethyl terephthalate? That's C10? Actually terephthalic acid dimethyl ester: C10H10O4? Not.

Let's compute carbon count for methyl 4-methoxy cinnamate (trans). Structure: phenyl with OMe para, attached to CH=CH-COOCH3. Carbons: phenyl 6, OMe carbon 1, CH=CH (2), carbonyl carbon 1, OCH3 carbon 1 = 11. Yes! That matches 11 carbons. So candidate: methyl 4-methoxycinnamate (also known as methyl p-anisate? Wait p-anisate is methyl p-methoxybenzoate (no double bond). Cinnamate adds CH=CH-COOCH3 (C3). So total 11.

Our carbon NMR: aromatic carbons 6 signals (some duplicates due to symmetry). 144.78 likely aromatic carbon attached to OMe (C-O). 132.00 maybe olefinic carbon (beta). 130.07 (two) maybe aromatic ortho/para? 127.80 (two) maybe other aromatic. Carbonyl 166.40. OCH3 at 52.24. Olefinic carbon (alpha) maybe 149? but we have 144.78 maybe aromatic. The olefinic carbons typical around 120-140. We have 130.07 and 127.80 duplicates maybe correspond to CH=CH. The aliphatic CH2? Actually cinnamate has no CH2, just CH=CH. So 49.55 and 43.55 and 19.23 maybe correspond to something else. But we have CH3 of OCH3 (52). The other aliphatic signals maybe from side chain? Wait methyl cinnamate has OCH3 (52), carbonyl (166), aromatic (6), olefinic (2). That's 9 signals. But we have 11 signals, extra two aliphatic signals (49.55, 43.55, 19.23). That's three extra. So maybe there is an ethoxy group (CH2CH3) giving CH2 ~ 60? Actually O-CH2-CH3: CH2 ~ 60, CH3 ~ 14. So 49.55 maybe CH2 attached to carbonyl (CH2-COO). 43.55 maybe CH2 adjacent to aromatic? Not.

Maybe compound is ethyl 4-methoxycinnamate (ethyl ester). That would have OCH2CH3: CH2 ~ 60, CH3 ~ 14. So we would have carbonyl (166), aromatic (6), olefinic (2), OCH3 on ring (52), OCH2 (60), CH3 (14). That's 12 carbons? Count: phenyl 6, OMe carbon 1, CH=CH (2), carbonyl carbon 1, OCH2 (1), CH3 (1) =12. Not 11.

Our data shows 11 carbons, with aliphatic signals at 52, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23. Could be OCH3 (52), CH2 (49.55), CH2 (43.55), CH3 (19.23). That's ethoxy plus maybe extra CH2? Could be propyl ester? Propyl would have CH2-CH2-CH3 (3 aliphatic). That matches 3 aliphatic signals. So maybe compound is propyl 4-methoxycinnamate (C12?). Count: phenyl 6, OMe 1, CH=CH 2, carbonyl 1, propyl (3) =13. Not.

Let's compute carbon count for propyl 4-methoxycinnamate: C13? Actually base cinnamate (C9H8O2) plus OMe (C1) plus propyl (C3) = C13. So not.

Our carbon count 11 suggests maybe there is a carbonyl (166), aromatic 6, OMe (52), and two aliphatic CH2 (49,43) and CH3 (19). That's 6+1+1+2+1 =11. So structure could be something like phenyl-CO-CH2-CH2-CH3? That's phenylacetone? But we also have OMe.

Maybe it's 4-methoxyphenylacetone (p-anisylacetone) = p-anisyl-CO-CH2-CH3? That would have aromatic 6, OMe carbon 1, carbonyl carbon 1, CH2 (1), CH3 (1) =10. Not.

What about 4-methoxyphenylpropanoic acid methyl ester? That would have aromatic 6, OMe 1, carbonyl 1, CH2-CH2-CH3 (3) =11. Yes! So methyl 4-methoxyphenylpropionate (also called methyl 4-methoxyphenylpropionate). Structure: aromatic ring with OMe para, attached to propanoate chain: -CH2-CH2-COOCH3? Wait methyl ester of 4-methoxyphenylpropionic acid: OMe on ring, side chain CH2-CH2-COOCH3 attached to ring via carbonyl? Actually phenylpropionic acid: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOH. Methyl ester: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3. Add OMe on ring. Carbons: phenyl 6, OMe 1, CH2 (attached to ring) 1, CH2 (next) 1, carbonyl carbon 1, OCH3 1 =11. Good. Aliphatic signals: CH2 attached to aromatic ~ 43 ppm, CH2 next to carbonyl ~ 49? maybe 43 and 49. OCH3 52. Methyl of ester 19. That matches.

Thus candidate SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CCCOC(=O)C? Wait need correct connectivity: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)OC? Wait carbonyl attached to CH2? Actually phenylpropionate: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CCCOC(=O)C? Wait carbonyl carbon is part of ester: OCH3 attached to carbonyl carbon. So chain: phenyl-CH2-CH2-C(=O)OCH3. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)OC. Need to ensure correct: COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)OC. Write as "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)OC". Remove spaces: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)OC". Wait that's phenyl-CH2-CH2-CH2-COOCH3 (propyl). Actually we need two CH2 then carbonyl. So "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)OC" where there are two C's before carbonyl: "COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)OC" would be phenyl-CH2-COOCH3 (phenylacetate). Need two CH2: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)OC". That's phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3? Actually "CCC(=O)OC" is propanoyl methyl ester (propionate). The chain is CH3-CH2-COOCH3. But we need phenyl attached to CH2-CH2-COOCH3, so phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3 is "COc1ccc(cc1)CC C(=O)OC"? Let's construct: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3: SMILES "COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)OC"? Wait that gives phenyl-CH2-COOCH3 (acetate). Because after phenyl we have "CC(=O)OC": first C is CH2 attached to phenyl, second C is carbonyl carbon. So only one CH2. Need two CH2: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)OC". Here phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3 (propionate). Yes.

Thus SMILES: "COc1ccc(cc1)CCC(=O)OC". Count carbons: OMe carbon (1), phenyl 6 =7, chain CH2-CH2 =2 =>9, carbonyl carbon =1 =>10, OCH3 carbon =1 =>11. Good.

Now validate mass: compute formula. Use tool.
